opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a tension I think about a lot. I have fairly strong views on some things. I've spent a long time on debate and scalable oversight, and I have an intuition about which theoretical problems are load-bearing. But I try to hold those views with a certain humility, because the track record of anyone confidently predicting which alignment approach will pan out is not great, including mine.

So the way I'd frame it is roughly a portfolio. You want some fraction of your effort going into the things the people leading the organisation think are most promising, because if you don't act on your best guesses, you're not really using your judgement at all. But you also want real diversification across bets that are meaningfully different: different assumptions about how capabilities develop, about whether we get warning shots, about whether interpretability scales, about whether theoretical guarantees are achievable or whether we'll be stuck with empirical safety cases.

One thing I've found useful is to ask, for each bet, "In what world does this turn out to be the thing that mattered?" If two projects only pay off in the same world, you're less diversified than you think. If a project pays off in a world I personally think is unlikely but not crazy, that can still be well worth funding, especially if nobody else is covering it.

The other piece is people. Researchers do their best work on problems they actually believe in. If I push everyone toward my favourite agenda, I get worse research from the people who don't share my intuitions, and I lose the error-correction that comes from having smart people who disagree with me in the building. So part of the job is creating space for people to pursue directions I'm sceptical of, while asking them to be clear about what would update them, and me, about whether it's working.

And finally, I try to be explicit about where my technical expectations are carrying the decision. If I'm deprioritising something because of a specific belief, say that some class of methods won't hold up against more capable models, I want that written down, so if the evidence changes we notice and shift rather than just running on inertia.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a diversified portfolio of meaningfully different research bets, including directions the speaker thinks are unlikely or is skeptical of.

r002.rationale: It says researchers need not share the speaker’s intuitions and argues for making space for people to pursue directions they disagree about.

r003.rationale: The response advocates diversification across bets; it does not suggest that a contribution from one research area could justify the organisation’s entire effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I do have fairly strong technical opinions, and I'm also aware that my track record of being right about which approach will pan out is... mixed. Everyone's is. Alignment is a field where the base rate of confident predictions being correct is not great, and I include myself in that.

So the way I'd frame it is that there are really two different jobs happening at once. One is the job of having a view: I have a picture of what I think the hard parts of the problem are, what I think is likely to work, where I think the leverage is. And that view should inform things. It would be strange to run a research organisation and have no opinion about what's worth doing. But the other job is more like portfolio management, where you're explicitly acknowledging that you're uncertain, that the field is uncertain, and that the right response to that is to fund a spread of bets rather than concentrate everything on the thing the person at the top happens to believe.

And I think the failure mode in both directions is real. If you lean too hard on the leader's technical expectations, you get a monoculture. Everyone works on the thing the boss finds compelling, people who disagree either leave or stop saying so, and if the boss is wrong, the whole organisation is wrong together, which is the worst possible way to be wrong. But if you lean too far the other way and say "we have no view, we'll just fund everything," you end up with no coherence, no ability to build on each other's work, and honestly a lot of mediocre research, because you've removed the thing that lets you say "no, that's not going to work, here's why."

So in practice, what I try to do is separate the question of "do I think this will work" from the question of "should we do this." Those are correlated, but they're not the same question. There are things I'm fairly sceptical of where I still think it's correct for us to have people working on them, because the cost of being wrong about that scepticism is high, and because there are other people in the organisation who are more excited about it than I am and who have good reasons. And conversely there are things I'm personally very into where I try to be honest that my enthusiasm shouldn't automatically translate into headcount.

The other thing I'd say is that the balance should probably shift over time and with scale. When you're small, you kind of have to concentrate, because you can't do five things well with eight people. As you grow, diversification gets cheaper and the cost of a single wrong bet gets larger, so you should naturally spread out more. And I'd also distinguish between bets that are different approaches to the same problem versus bets on different problems entirely. The first kind I'm quite happy to spread across. The second kind, where someone says "actually the whole framing of what matters is wrong," those are more expensive to support but arguably the most important ones to make room for, because that's where your blind spots are.

I'll admit I don't think I've fully solved this. The honest answer is that my technical views do shape things more than a purely neutral portfolio allocation would, and I think that's partly correct and partly a bias I should keep an eye on. The thing I try to hold onto is that the point isn't for the organisation to reflect my beliefs. The point is for the organisation to be more likely to be right than I am on my own, and that requires it to disagree with me somewhere.

r001.rationale: The response recommends spreading research bets because leadership is uncertain, including support for approaches the leader is skeptical of.

r002.rationale: It argues for a coherent research organization and does not say researchers need not share a view of how approaches fit together.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that a sufficiently important contribution from one research area could justify the organization’s efforts.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to distinguish between having a technical view and making that view a requirement for everyone in the organisation. I should be able to say, “Here’s why I expect this approach to work, and here are the problems I see with that other approach.” But people should be able to disagree with me and pursue something on the strength of their arguments.

That doesn’t mean spreading resources equally across every possible bet. You need some judgment about which directions are promising, and enough concentration that people can actually make progress. But my personal expectations shouldn’t be the only input into that judgment. In particular, you want people who can lead research directions that I wouldn’t have come up with, or whose promise I don’t yet fully understand.

The useful question is then: what would we learn from pursuing this? What result would make us more excited, and what would make us change course? That gives you a way to have a coherent research organisation while still allowing genuine disagreement about how alignment is going to work.

r001.rationale: The response says personal expectations should not be the only input and supports pursuing promising directions led by people whose ideas Irving would not have developed or fully understood.

r002.rationale: It allows researchers to disagree with Irving, but does not say they need not share a view of how the research approaches fit together.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that a sufficiently important contribution from one research area could justify the organisation’s overall efforts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to distinguish between having a technical view and making everyone work on that view. You need some expectations about what’s likely to work in order to make decisions, but those expectations should be open to revision.

So I’d want people to understand why I’m excited about a direction, and also to have room to pursue approaches I’m less convinced by, if they have a strong argument. The important thing is that those bets come with some account of what we could learn: what would make us more optimistic, what would make us less optimistic, and how that would change what we do next.

There’s a balance there. If everyone pursues unrelated ideas, you lose the benefits of working together. But if the organisation just amplifies the leader’s intuitions, you can end up with a lot of people making essentially the same mistake. I’d aim for enough shared direction that people can help each other, with enough independence that my technical expectations don’t become the boundary of what we investigate.

r001.rationale: It supports pursuing approaches Irving is less convinced by when researchers have strong arguments, giving the organisation bets beyond his personal expectations.

r002.rationale: It allows room for independent approaches, but also calls for enough shared direction; it does not say researchers need not share a view of how the approaches fit together.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that a contribution from one research area could justify the organisation’s entire effort.
